newsitem.title: UK: PEPs, TESSAs are safe with UK Labour, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: PEPs, TESSAs are safe with UK Labour, analysts say.

text.p: Britons who have invested billions of pounds in tax-free PEPs and TESSAs can breathe easy -- a Labour government might encourage them to hold on to their savings for longer but dramatic change is unlikely, analysts said.
However, industry players do expect some alteration to the rules governing these Personal Equity Plans (PEPs) and Tax Exempt Special Savings Accounts (TESSAs) if Labour wins the May 1 election.

In its manifesto the opposition Labour Party -- which is way ahead in the opinion polls -- said it would "introduce a new individual savings account and extend the principle of TESSAs and PEPs to promote long-term saving".
This means the existing system of PEPs and TESSAs should be safe under Labour, at least in the near future.

"They (Labour) will not substantially alter the PEP format until they know what they want to put in its place," Philip Warland, director general of the Association of Unit Trusts and Investment Funds (AUTIF), said.
Tony Blair's Labour has to date given few details of exactly what its individual savings account will involve.
Warland said Labour might make such a tax-favoured account limited in its uses, earmarked for things like retirement, long-term care or possibly even healthcare.
But it is unlikely to make drastic changes to PEPs and TESSAs, which have been one of the Conservative government's success stories since they were introduced in the 1980s.
PEPs were aimed at bringing fresh investors into the equity market and around 35 billion pounds ($57 billion) have been invested in them since they were introduced in 1987.
They have encouraged many people to save for the longer-term, and can now be linked by financial services providers with mortgages.

Individuals have been able to invest up to 9,000 pounds a year in PEPs, including 3,000 that can be invested in the shares of a single company, but there have been suggestions that a Labour government might choose to reduce the overall total.
PEPs have been criticised for allowing wealthier investors to shelter hundreds of thousands of pounds from the taxman while the cost to the Inland Revenue keeps rising.
For the 1996-97 financial year the cost of income tax relief and capital gains tax exemption for PEP investments was estimated by the Inland Revenue at 600 million pounds.
Some analyts suggest that a Labour, or for that matter a future Conservative, government could withdraw the 3,000 pound annual single company PEP allowance.
This scheme has been used for what one source described as "recognised abuses", with offshore investment companies being set up simply as a vehicle for tax-free savings.
Another way of clawing back some of the lost tax would be to impose a limit on the amount invested. The less wealthy would still be encouraged to invest in such schemes, analysts said.

Tony Baker, deputy director general of the Association of British Insurers (ABI), believes that Labour will want to find something positive to put into the special Budget it has pledged to bring in within two months of being elected.
He said that the individual savings account would be particularly positive for people "of relatively modest means".
But simplicity would be central if people are to be encouraged to put money aside.
A Labour government would be keen to avoid any upfront cost to such a scheme, so the tax benefits were unlikely to be immediate.

Baker said Labour, which has promised not to increase income tax if elected, is also unlikely to impose any radical changes in insurance products, but it may be tempted to increase the tax on insurance premiums for motor and household policies.

"I don't think there will be dramatic changes...but there could be pressure to increase insurance premium tax on non-life products," he said, adding that such an increase, which would bring Britain more in line with Europe, would hit the less well-off hardest. ($ = 0.614 British Pounds)
